headline: Mother was papa, drifted to hawa, then a doubled sound pulled it back to haha in the late 16th century.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese papa, in turn traced to Proto-Japonic *papa.
/haha/: */papa/ → /fafa/ → /fawa/ → /fafa/ → /haha/.
First cited to a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 729, with the phonetic spelling 婆婆 (papa).

Medial /f/ [ɸ] regularly changes to /w/ [ɰᵝ], resulting in /fawa/ → /hawa/, the expected final form; see hawa below. This form first appears in the Heian period. However, likely due to spelling influence or reduplication associations, the earlier /fafa/ resurfaced in the late 16th century towards the end of the Muromachi period, with both forms seen until recent times, when hawa falls into disuse. Initial /f-/ [ɸ] regularly becomes [h], resulting in modern [ha̠ha̠].

headline: Father is a doubled syllable too: Old Japanese titi, Proto-Japonic *titi.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 父 (titi), from Proto-Japonic *titi.
Still in modern usage.

headline: Elder brother is perhaps “my” + の + “eldest sibling”: 吾 (a) + の (no) + 兄 (ye), though the source calls it unclear.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
* Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) + の (no, possessive particle) + 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”, see below):
*: ⟨a no₂ ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ani/
* Alternatively, an apophonic form of 姉 (ane, “elder sister”), itself possibly from the same derivation above.
* Several other theories have also been suggested.

headline: Elder sister (ane) and elder brother (ani) may be apophonic twins; the source says the derivation is unclear.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
* Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) + の (no, possessive particle) + 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”):
*: ⟨a no₂ ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ane/
* An apophonic form of 兄 (ani, “elder brother”).
* Several other theories have also been suggested.

headline: Imōto was imo + hito: a u-sound shift glued “sister” and “person” together.

sources.quote: ⟨imo₁⟩ → */imʷo/ → /imo/
From Old Japanese 妹 (imo₁). First cited in the Kojiki of 712.

Speculatively, may be related to terms such as 女 (me₁, womi₁na, “woman”), 嫗 (omi₁na, “elderly woman”), and 母 (omo, “mother”), wherein the medial /-m-/ appears to signify woman, female. However, the difference in vowel values presents a difficulty.
/imo ɸito/ → /imowito/ → */imowuto/ → /imoːto/
Originally a compound of 妹 (imo, “sister, close female companion”) + 人 (hito, “person”). First cited in The Tales of Ise of the early 900s.

This is an instance of ウ音便 (u onbin, “u sound shift”), found in terms with bilabial consonants (/m/, /b/, /w/) followed by i; commonly seen in terms such as 玄人 (kurōto, “professional”), 素人 (shirōto, “amateur”), or possibly, 相撲 (sumō, “sumo”).

headline: Yūbe, “last night”, is a shift from 夕べ (“evening”), and its kanji spelling comes from sakuya.

sources.quote: Shift from 夕べ (yūbe, “evening”), which has an additional 平板型 (heiban-gata) or [0] accent pitch.
The kanji spelling is from sakuya above.
Cognate with Northern Amami Ōshima ゆぶぃ (yubï, “last night”).

headline: Shōgatsu is borrowed from Middle Chinese 正月 (tsyeng ngjwot).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 正月 (MC tsyeng ngjwot)

headline: Kita is Old Japanese, but its ultimate derivation is unknown.

sources.quote: Attributed to Old Japanese, although the exact phonetics are not clear, as the term is not cited in phonetic man'yōgana.
Ultimate derivation unknown.

headline: Okane is just 御 (o-, beautifying prefix) plus 金 (kane, “money”).

sources.quote: 御(お) (o-, beautifying prefix) + 金(かね) (kane, “money”).

headline: Utsukushii was utsukushi, before its ending became しき (shiki) and then the medial k fell out.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 美(うつく)し (utsukushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii). Most likely related to 厳しい (itsukushii, “beautiful, pretty”).

headline: Nigai was nigashi in Early Middle Japanese, before its ending was replaced and the medial k fell out.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 苦(にが)し (nigashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *ninka; cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *niga.
First cited to a text from 858.

headline: Ōi is cognate with 大きい (ōkii, “big”), and with Proto-Ryukyuan *opo.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *əpə. Cognate with 大きい (ōkii, “big, large”) and Proto-Ryukyuan *opo (whence Okinawan 多さん (ufusan)).

meaning: a painting; a picture; a drawing
headline: E was we in Middle Chinese 繪, the goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 繪 (MC hwajH). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Compare Wu 繪 /绘 (⁶we).

meaning: to cut; to hang up (a phone)
headline: Kiru is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kiru, with Ryūkyūan cognates.

sources.quote: ⟨ki₁ru⟩ → */kjiru/ → /kiru/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kiru. Cognate with Miyako 切 (きぃー, ksïï), Okinawan 切ーん (ちーん, chīn), Yaeyama 切すん (きぃすん, kïsun).

meaning: entrance (to a house or a building)
headline: Genkan was earlier genkwan; the source notes it was common during the Edo period.

sources.quote: /ɡenkwan/ → /ɡenkan/.
From earlier genkan. genkwan > genkwa > genka. The final /a/ was likely nasalized. Common during the Edo period.

headline: Suzushii may ultimately derive from onomatopoeia; compare 涼む (suzumu, “to cool down”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 涼し (sususi, suzusi, “cold, refreshing, cool”), following シク活用 (shiku katsuyō, “-shiku conjugation”). First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and the Man'yōshū, completed sometime after 759 CE.
May ultimately derive from onomatopoeia. Compare 涼む (suzumu, “to cool down”).

meaning: if I remember correctly; certain, definite
headline: Tashika derives from the tashi- element in たしに (tashi ni, “sufficiently; firmly; surely”) plus the suffix か (-ka).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Derived from the tashi- element seen in たしに (tashi ni, “sufficiently; firmly; surely”) and たしない (tashinai, “difficult, agonizing; poor, lacking”) + adjective-forming suffix か (-ka).

headline: Mukō has two possible sources, both from a nominalization of the verb 向かう (mukau, “to face”).

sources.quote: Two possible sources:

* From a nominalization of the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “terminal form”) or 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”). The modern pronunciation would suggest that the morpheme boundary in the original verb muka.u has been lost.

* From a nominalization of the ウ音(おん)便(びん) (u-onbin, “u euphonic change”) form of 向(む)かい (mukai, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”)), compare dialectal forms like 向(む)こうて (mukōte).
Accordingly, the historical kana spellings should be むかふ (mukafu) according to the former, and むかう (mukau) according to the latter. Compare 相撲(すもう) (sumō), of similar derivation.

meaning: to search, to seek, to look for
headline: Sagasu is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sankasu.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sankasu.

headline: Gaikokujin is, by surface analysis, 外国 (gaikoku, “foreign country”) plus 人 (-jin, “person”).

sources.quote: /ɡwaikokuzin/ → /ɡaikokudʑin/
By surface analysis, 外国(がいこく) (gaikoku, “foreign country”) + 人(じん) (-jin, “person”).

headline: Umi is theorized to be 大 (ō-, “big”) plus 水 (mi, “water”), though the source finds that problematic.

sources.quote: ⟨umi₁⟩ → */umij/ → /umi/
From Old Japanese, theorized as descending from Proto-Japonic *omi.
Has been thought to have been derived from a compound. There are two leading theories regarding the ultimate derivation:
* Shift from 大 (ō-, “big, great”) + 水 (mi, “water”, combining form).
: This is problematic phonetically because there is no known term having a related shift from /opo/ → /oː/ → /o/ → /u/, and semantically as there already exists a compound 大水 (ōmizu, “flood”).

* From う (u-, stem indicating “ocean”) + 水 (mi, “water”, combining form). The u- stem is evident in 魚 (uo, “fish”) and 潮 (ushio, “salt water; tide”), and in the 海 (una) element in various ancient terms (see below).

headline: Hana went /pana/ → /fana/ → /hana/, from Proto-Japonic *pana.

sources.quote: /pana/ → /fana/ → /hana/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pana.

headline: Uriba is 売り (uri, “selling”) plus 場 (ba, “place”), attested since at least 1595.

sources.quote: Compound of 売(う)り (uri, “selling”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 売(う)る (uru, “to sell”)) + 場(ば) (ba, “place”).
Attested since at least 1595.

headline: Onna was womina in Old Japanese, then omina, and the source traces womi1na → womʉna → wonːa → onːa.

sources.quote: ⟨womi₁na⟩ → */womʲina/ → /womʉna/ → /wonːa/ → /onːa/
Shift from Old Japanese womina → omina. See the 女 (omina) entry for further details.
Now one of the standard Japanese words for "a woman".

headline: Uta is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ota.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ota.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Ima is first attested in the Kojiki, and one proposal splits it into i (“this”) plus ma.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *ima. Frellesvig suggests a compound of reconstructed proximal demonstrative *i (compare Middle Korean 이 (i, “this”)) + ma (corresponding to modern 間(ま) (ma, “space”).

headline: Shiraseru is the causative form of the verb 知る (shiru, “to know”).

sources.quote: The causative form of verb 知る (shiru, “to know”).

headline: Byōin is 病 (byō, “illness”) plus 院 (-in, “institution”).

sources.quote: From 病(びょう) (byō, “illness”) + 院(いん) (-in, “institution”).

headline: Ryūgakusei is 留学 (ryūgaku) plus 生 (-sei).

sources.quote: 留学(りゅうがく) (ryūgaku) + 生(せい) (-sei)

headline: Nigeru is from Old Japanese 逃ぐ (nigu), from Proto-Japonic *nink-ai-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 逃ぐ (nigu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *nink-ai-.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Okashi is 御 (o-, polite prefix) plus 菓子 (kashi, “confection”).

sources.quote: From 御 (o-, polite prefix) + 菓子 (kashi, “confection”).
